newsitem.title: USA: U.S. debt futures end up, Sept bonds end at 112-02.
newsitem.headline: U.S. debt futures end up, Sept bonds end at 112-02.

text.p: U.S. debt futures extended Friday's gains in thin volume, with September T-bonds settling at last Friday's high of 112-02/32.
"I think the market is overbought, but in the absence of any bad news what's to drive yields up?" Sharon Alister, broker and senior vice president at Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc, said.

September T-bonds inched up to 112-07/32, the contract's highest level since February 20 when it traded at 112-16/32, after initially stalling at 112-02/32. Volume was lighter than normal, floor traders and analysts said.
"You do have to respect the price action," one T-bond futures trader said. "It feels like the sellers have no power in here."
Alister attributed the day's gains to heavy liquidity.
"There is just a lot of liquidity around that needs to get invested," she said. "And your choices are the stock and bond markets."

Traders and analysts speculated that foreign money started to rush into U.S. asset markets after the Socialist victory in French elections. The results of the elections heightened uncertainty about the fate of the single European currency.
In addition, U.S. economic numbers last week continued to show that growth remained strong, while U.S. inflationary pressures mild.
"Everything is right with the world," one trader said.

U.S. Treasury secretary Robert Rubin said on Monday that the U.S. economy was thriving partly because the federal deficit has fallen to about one percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) from nearly five percent in 1993.
"These are the best sustained economic concditions in this country in many decades, and the best in the industrialized worl," Rubin said in a speech.
His speech was prepared for delivery to the Bretton Woods/Overseas Development Council.
Rubin said one U.S. objective at the Group of Seven (G7) meeting on June 20-22 in Denver will be to promote growth in order to keep the global economy thriving.
One trader said the results of a booming U.S. economy were reflected by the heavy increase in U.S. tax receipts and the decline in the budget deficit.
"The Treasury's decision not to auction 10-year notes could be arousing concerns about a lack of supply," he said.

Traders will be looking closely at Tuesday's line-up of U.S. economic indicators. The U.S. May Consumer Price Index (CPI) is seen rising 0.2 percent overall and in the core rate, versus up 0.1 percent overall and up 0.3 percent excluding food and energy in April.
CPI and housing starts, which are forecast to fall slightly to an annual rate of 1.47 million units, compared to 1.473 million units, will be released at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.

At the end of pit trade, September T-bonds were up 07/32 at 112-02/32, 10-year notes were up 05/32 at 108-18/32, T-bills were up 0.015 at 94.805, December Eurodollars were up 0.005 at 93.97, and munibonds were up 09/32 at 116-18/32. ((DerivativesDesk(312)408-8750)) E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com
